content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
The paper proposes a network architecture for video-to-video translation. The architecture is essentially an encoder-decoder  with recurrent units in the latent space for modeling the motion dynamics.  

The paper is quite poorly written. 
- The title doesn't say much about what is in the paper.
- The paper is barely motivated and it seems that the goal of the paper is just to improve the video to video translation quality for no good reason. 
- Related work study is mixed with the introduction in a not coherent way.
- The main contributions of the paper is not clearly stated.
- In the experimentation section, there is almost no analysis of the results to provide reader with insights. 
- The strongest point of the paper is their experimentation which still can be improved. All of the experiments are on a SINGLE dataset which makes the quantitative results less than acceptable. 
- For a video paper, unfortunately the authors did not provide any video (in the forms of supplementary material) which makes qualitative compression hard as well. 
- The authors compared their model to an "Improved Recycle-GAN" but they did not provide any details on what this version is!
- Comparison with vid2vid is missing from Table 3 to 5 and only appears in Table 6. 

Overall, the paper (in the current written form) is weak with marginal contribution at best, surely not suitable for a top conference such as ICLR. Only weak rejecting the paper since this is not my primary area of research (although I'm quite familiar with it), so maybe I'm missing something ...

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and addressed your concerns as follows:

-The title doesn't say much about what is in the paper.
We aim to keep the title short and put emphasis on the key element of our work — we use self-supervised learning to capture the abundant structure information within the video data, to solve the unpaired video translation problem.

-The paper is barely motivated and it seems that the goal of the paper is just to improve the video to video translation quality for no good reason. 
As we have discussed in our introduction, the contribution of this paper is twofold: 1) we decompose content and style for controllable and long-term consistent video translation, 2) we propose a video interpolation loss to train our recurrent video translator in a self-supervised manner. The effect of the two contributions have been validated in our ablation study.

-Related work study is mixed with the introduction in a not coherent way.
-The main contributions of the paper is not clearly stated.
Due to the limitation of the pages, we merged the introduction and the related work. As both the reviewer 1 and 3 have suggested us to split the introduction and related works, we will introduce a related work section in our future version to make our contribution more clearer.


- In the experimentation section, there is almost no analysis of the results to provide reader with insights. 
We have provided very detailed ablation studies in our manuscript to discuss the effects of different components in our model.

- The strongest point of the paper is their experimentation which still can be improved. All of the experiments are on a SINGLE dataset which makes the quantitative results less than acceptable. 
We have evaluated our model on the Viper and Cityscapes datasets, the experimental results of translating videos from the Cityscapes dataset to the Viper dataset can be found in our submitted appendix.


- For a video paper, unfortunately the authors did not provide any video (in the forms of supplementary material) which makes qualitative compression hard as well. 
The GIF videos for qualitative comparison are attached in the following links: https://uvitvid2vid.github.io/UvitCompare1/UvitCompare1.html

- The authors compared their model to an "Improved Recycle-GAN" but they did not provide any details on what this version is!
As RecycleGAN only constraints motion between two adjacent frames and not able to generate long-term consistent video, we use our style-content decomposition strategy to improve RecycleGAN. We have introduced why and how we compare our method with improved RecycleGAN, please refer to 3.1 Quantitative Analysis, Label-to-image mapping part for more details. 


- Comparison with vid2vid is missing from Table 3 to 5 and only appears in Table 6. 
Vid2vid model is a supervised model, while the proposed UVIT is an unsupervised model. We provide the human preference score of Vid2vid to show that the visual quality of translation results by UVIT is comparable with a supervised model. While for other experiments, we do not think it is necessary to compare unsupervised methods with the supervised method.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
SUMMARY: Perform unsupervised/self-supervised image-to-label and label-to-image translation on the Viper dataset

CLAIMS:
- Perform self-supervised training
- Have consistency in long-term style and short-term content

LIT REVIEW: Sufficient literature review for the task at hand.

DECISION: Good work, but paper needs a lot of improvement

The work done and effort put to get good results seem worthwhile. The idea is simple enough, but slightly hacky, in the sense that they use cycle-consistency in style domain (as is done with images in a lot of literature), but improve upon RecycleGAN by adding a recurrent neural network to consume multiple frames instead of just one. In addition, possibly to improve the representation learnt, they combine with an interpolation loss, which is another common idea in video literature. It seems like there needs to be a more coherent idea to string the work together. If it is a pure combination of different methods to make the results work, the authors can mention so.

The writing is not clear, and it seems hasty. A lot more time could have been spent on making the story clearer, having a better explanation of the method. The method seems to be explained in parts in the introduction and in later sections. It would be better to explain it fully in one section instead of in parts.

It is also not clear that there are two tasks being tackled - interpolation and translation - to achieve the overall objective, I had to realize it myself as I was reading. There is no clear explanation provided as to why interpolation is being done if the overall task is translation. It could be that interpolation is an excellent task to discover good content in videos in a self-supervised manner, but it is not mentioned anywhere in the paper.

Sufficient experiments have been done to prove that their method works better than previous methods, on the Viper dataset on translation between images and their semantic segmentation labels. However, the claims of being long-term consistent in style is not explicitly shown in a quantitative manner, it is only perhaps shown qualitatively. First of all, it is not clear what the authors mean when they say "long-term": how many frames is the threshold between short-term and long-term according to the authors? Since the translation task is conditioned on style, it need not be that the new style is "consistent" in the long term, it is simply conditioned upon. It is one way of tackling "long-term consistency", but not very satisfactory.

There are several mistakes in the content of the paper. The math used is very weak and unnecessary, In my opinion it is alright not to have detailed math, but it is not good to express it badly. The conditional formulations are very wrong, I would advise the authors to recheck the expressions.

Unfortunately, it is not possible to verify how good the method is until:
1) examples of the videos are shown, and not just images. This could be done by making a website and uploading example videos.
2) the code is released.

content.title: Response (part1)
content.comment:
The writing is not clear, and it seems hasty. A lot more time could have been spent on making the story clearer, having a better explanation of the method. The method seems to be explained in parts in the introduction and in later sections. It would be better to explain it fully in one section instead of in parts.

Due to the limitation of the pages, we merged the introduction and the related work. As both the reviewer 1 and 2 have suggested us to split the introduction and related works, we will introduce a related work section in our future version to make our contribution clearer.

It is also not clear that there are two tasks being tackled - interpolation and translation - to achieve the overall objective, I had to realize it myself as I was reading. There is no clear explanation provided as to why interpolation is being done if the overall task is translation. It could be that interpolation is an excellent task to discover good content in videos in a self-supervised manner, but it is not mentioned anywhere in the paper.

There are mainly two motivations of using the video interpolation as the auxiliary task to help the video translation:

First, video interpolation adds internal constraints for better combination of the information used in the translation task. In the video translation process, the content used for translation is produced by combining the inter-frame content (propagated by RNNs) and the current frame content. Inter-frame content information helps to build up dependency between the current frame and its surrounding frames, ensuring content consistency across frames. However, if inter-frame content and current frame content are not aligned well, image-level quality can be influenced. The combined translation frame will incline to over smooth the image-level details and sacrifice the high-level semantic correspondence with the specific input frame. By using current frame content to supervise the inter-frame content, the video interpolation loss aims to constrain the inter-frame content information so that it can be combined with content from the current frame more organically. Therefore, the translation process directly benefits from the interpolation process. 

Second, video interpolation and video translation share the same building blocks. Such self-supervised training would be beneficial for the building blocks to make the network more stable. For example, TrajGRUs are the modules responsible for capturing motion information across frames. However, RNNs are notoriously difficult to train, especially in the unpaired setting. Recently, Trinh et al. [1] suggest that simultaneously learning supervised and unsupervised tasks can enhance an RNN’s ability to capture dependencies. The video interpolation task is crucial to help TrajGRUs  actively learn the location-variant structure in the video data. 


[1] Trinh, Trieu H., et al. "Learning longer-term dependencies in rnns with auxiliary losses." arXiv preprint arXiv:1803.00144 (2018).

content.title: Response(part2)
content.comment:
Q:
 The work done and effort put to get good results seem worthwhile. The idea is simple enough, but slightly hacky, in the sense that they use cycle-consistency in style domain (as is done with images in a lot of literature), but improve upon RecycleGAN by adding a recurrent neural network to consume multiple frames instead of just one. In addition, possibly to improve the representation learnt, they combine with an interpolation loss, which is another common idea in video literature. It seems like there needs to be a more coherent idea to string the work together. If it is a pure combination of different methods to make the results work, the authors can mention so.

A:
Previous methods fail to produce style consistent and multimodal video sequences. Besides, they lack the ability to achieve translation which is both content consistent enough and framewise realistic. To tackle these limitations, we rethink about the integrated solution:

Style control: the idea of using style code for controllable translation has already been adopted in some previous image translation works. Under the assumption that close frames share the same style information, we adopt the same style code to generate the whole video. As we have validated in our ablation study, this is a highly effective way to generate style consistent video sequence.

Recurrent translator: RNN is a powerful architecture for capturing long-term information, however, the training of RNN is also more difficult than CNN. Previously, the difficulty of training RNN has impeded the application of RNN in the challenging unsupervised video2video translation works. While the powerful video interpolation loss enables UVIT to adopt RNN translator to ensure image level quality as well as video-level consistency.

Video interpolation loss: the video interpolation loss has been adopted in some previous works to learn image/video representation, while, in this paper, we utilize it to provide pixel-level supervision for training our video translator. Please note that the video interpolation loss can not be applied to train previous unsupervised video translators, e.g. 3D cycleGAN and RecycleGAN, the special conditional RNN encoder-decoder architecture enables us to train our translator with video interpolation loss. 

To summarize, the proposed UVIT approach is not a simple combination of existing techniques, it is a novel framework which utilizes self-supervised learning so that the translated frame can combine inter-frame information and current frame information coherently.



Q: 
Sufficient experiments have been done to prove that their method works better than previous methods, on the Viper dataset on translation between images and their semantic segmentation labels. However, the claims of being long-term consistent in style is not explicitly shown in a quantitative manner, it is only perhaps shown qualitatively. First of all, it is not clear what the authors mean when they say "long-term": how many frames is the threshold between short-term and long-term according to the authors? Since the translation task is conditioned on style, it need not be that the new style is "consistent" in the long term, it is simply conditioned upon. It is one way of tackling "long-term consistency", but not very satisfactory.


A:
The primary motivation for adopting the style-content decomposition is to achieve style consistency for long video sequences. We agree that it is more proper to call it style conditioned instead of long-term style consistency. For the experiment, we tried sequences up to 240 frames, which are easy to extend longer. They are style consistent qualitatively. In our training process, 6 frames are loaded together in one batch to capture the short-term content consistency.

There are several mistakes in the content of the paper. The math used is very weak and unnecessary, In my opinion it is alright not to have detailed math, but it is not good to express it badly. The conditional formulations are very wrong, I would advise the authors to recheck the expressions.

To highlight the crucial part and avoid distraction by the details, we will reorganize equations and math expressions.

Q:
Unfortunately, it is not possible to verify how good the method is until:
1) examples of the videos are shown, and not just images. This could be done by making a website and uploading example videos.
2) the code is released.

A:
The GIF videos for qualitative comparison are attached in the following links: https://uvitvid2vid.github.io/UvitCompare1/UvitCompare1.html. We’ll clean the code and release it in the future.

content.review:
This paper presents a new way for video to video translation with style control.
The author claims to have a better optimization objective with interpolation and style encoder loss.
A. It would be good to provide video supplementary materials for generated videos. From the generated images,
It is hard to compare the performance with RecycleGAN.
C. The interpolation loss is not very innovative, it is a light variation of recycle loss in RecycleGAN.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and addressed your concerns as follows:

A. It would be good to provide video supplementary materials for generated videos. From the generated images, It is hard to compare the performance with RecycleGAN.
The GIF videos for qualitative comparison are attached in the following links: https://uvitvid2vid.github.io/UvitCompare1/UvitCompare1.html 
The results of Human Preference Score are reported using GIF videos evaluated by Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT).

C. The interpolation loss is not very innovative, it is a light variation of recycle loss in RecycleGAN.
We argue that video interpolation loss is essentially different from Recycle loss from the following three aspects:

1)Temporal information incorporating: RecycleGAN uses supervised trained video predictor to capture the motion between two adjacent frames, while our RNN-based method captures temporal information from more frames.
2)Better supervision: In the RecycleGAN method, the predictor works as a fixed building block to bridge two adjacent frames and only constraints the generated frames to fulfill the estimated motion constraint. Such a simple motion constraint between two images is weak, two flat frames with the same value also fulfill the motion constraint. As a result, RecycleGAN still mainly relies on the GAN loss and motion constraint can only alleviate the inter-frame flickering problem. While, in our UVIT method, we use the same network (with different input and style code) for video translation and interpolation. The interpolation loss provides pixel-level supervision for training all the building blocks in our translator, it helps to stabilize the training process of UVIT and subsequently improve the final translation results. 
3)Directly helping the translation process: In RecycleGAN, the final frames of a specific sequence are produced by the image translator independently. The translator itself is a very traditional image domain translator, without the ability to record the inter-frame information. While in our model, the translation process directly benefits from the temporal information tailored in interpolation process. The content used for translation is produced by combining the inter-frame content (propagated by RNNs) and the current frame content.  By using current frame content to supervise the inter-frame content, the video interpolation loss aims to constrain the inter-frame information so that it can be combined with the current frame content more organically. Thanks to this, our model can produce sharp and semantic preserving frames.
As pointed out in the Future Work part of RecycleGAN [1], their model is limited in capturing the inter-frame information, thus could not learn the motion (e.g. speed) of the output. Our model use spatiotemporal generative models, which allow us to learn the motion of generated output.

Aayush Bansal, Shugao Ma, Deva Ramanan, and Yaser Sheikh. Recycle-gan: Unsupervised video retargeting. In Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), pages 119–135, 2018.


D. Typos are quite a few, for example, in figure. 1: translatier...
Thanks for pointing out, we will check our paper carefully to correct our typos.

E. Please help re-examine the equation. Why in the optimization procedure, minimizing the discriminator
In our paper, we utilized the relativistic gan (RGAN) method for training our model and followed the formulation of RGAN. Specifically, we formulate the losses for generator and discriminator separately,  minimizing the loss for the discriminator is equivalent to maximizing the GAN loss for the generator part.
